title: Kalidasa's Shakuntala — the Sanskrit text
author: kalidasa
attributionNote: The drama of Kālidāsa in seven acts, drawn from the Shakuntala episode of the Mahabharata and the story of the ring that reveals the heroine to her husband; it was the first Sanskrit work translated into a European language, by William Jones in 1789. GRETIL's e-text follows M. R. Kale's edition (Bombay 1898; ninth edition 1961).
description: Abhijñānaśākuntala tells of Shakuntala, the daughter of the sage Vishvamitra and the nymph Menaka, who grows up in the forest hermitage of Kanva; of king Dushyanta, who meets her there, marries her in the manner of the forest and returns to his city; of the ring he has given her, lost in a river and swallowed by a fish, without which he cannot remember her; of her rejection at court and the birth of her son Bharata in the hermitage of Marichi; and of the reunion when the ring is recovered and the king recognises his wife and the child who is to be the ancestor of the epic's kings. Its seven acts turn a memory into a drama of what is lost and found, and its heroine became the model of the Indian stage.
historicalContext: The play represents the classic form of Sanskrit drama — the nāṭaka in seven acts, with its vidūṣaka, its aerial journeys and its happy ending — and its translation by William Jones in 1789 began the European reading of Indian literature; Goethe's epigram on Shakuntala and the play's enthusiasm in Germany and Russia made it the most famous Indian literary work in the West.
availabilityNote: Complete as GRETIL publishes it: all seven acts with their verses and prose, streamed from GRETIL at read time, one act at a time. The file marks each verse and each prose speech with the act's reference, so a chapter holds the passages in the order the edition prints them. This is the original Sanskrit, not a translation.
